entry.title: judgement over volume
entry.summary: Day four of a hundred: a website concept for Nina Estate in Málaga that reads less like a property portal and more like a private practice, with the director, the method and four residences up front.
entry.content:
On 20 November I posted the fourth note of this run, the challenge Ramiah Trask set: a hundred days, a hundred businesses, a hundred websites. Day one was a family builder in the Marina Alta who needed a first clear page. That page is here. Day two was a theatre in Málaga with a full season and no order to it. That one is here. Day three was a family restaurant in my own town, with many reasons to walk in. That one is here. Today the business sells something people take months to decide on.

Nina Estate is a real estate agency in Málaga, with an office on Avenida de Cánovas del Castillo. It works across the city and the Costa del Sol: homes, whole buildings, investments and long-term rentals. It already has a website, at ninaestate.com, which sets out its experience, its properties and its services. My concept is here: Nina Estate, day four.

This is an independent redesign. It is not a collaboration with Nina Estate, nobody there asked for it, and nothing on the page means they approve of it. It lives on my own address for now, like the three before it.

a different kind of agency page

Most property websites are built like shop windows. A search bar at the top, a grid of listings, a price on every card, a phone number in the corner. That works for an agency that wins on volume, with hundreds of homes and a buyer who wants to scroll.

Nina Estate is a different shape of business. A small number of properties, several of them whole buildings. Prices on request. One person, the director, who deals with every client herself. Somebody buying or selling at that level of the luxury market is not mainly choosing a listing. They are choosing who they trust to choose for them.

So I took a different approach from the existing site. Less like a traditional agency, more like a private practice, where the way things are presented, the personal service and the attention to detail are part of what the client gets. The existing site leads with experience, properties and services. The concept leads with the relationship: who you will deal with, how the search will go, and what happens from the first call to the keys.

The idea is simple to say. The website should feel closer to the service it sells.

residences of quiet distinction

The opening is mostly empty, on purpose. A headline in a large, light serif: residences of quiet distinction, with the second line in italic. A small line in oxblood under it reads Málaga, Marbella, Costa del Sol. On the right is one sentence that does the job of a mission statement: a private real estate practice for buyers, sellers and investors who value judgement over volume.

Below that is one wide photograph, labelled Plate I, as in a book: a villa at dusk, the pool lit, bougainvillea over the terrace, lanterns on the low wall. The page holds it at that size and puts nothing on top of it.

Under the photograph, where most agency sites would put a search form with a dozen fields, there is a sentence to complete. I would like to buy a villa in Marbella. Each of the three words in italic is a menu. Buy can become rent, invest in or sell. Villa can become house, apartment or building. Marbella can become Málaga Centro, El Limonar or the Costa del Sol. Then one button: view residences.

It is a small thing, and it changes the tone. A search form asks you to filter. A sentence asks what you want, in the way an agent would on the phone. In the concept the sentence leads to the residences. It does not pretend to run a search the business does not need.

The opening, cut in two. The same welcome in daylight and after dark.

stone, ink and oxblood

The colours come from what this market already looks like when it is done well: plaster, old paper, dark wood, a glass of red on a table.

The light theme is warm stone, #DEDBD5, with near-black ink, #141312, for the text, and oxblood, #6E2323, for the small things that matter: the numbers, the active filter, the italic words in the sentence. The dark theme is almost black, #121110, with off-white text, #ECE7E0, and a muted rose, #D9A79B, where the oxblood was. Neither is the main version. They are two complete sites, and the same residence has to look right in both.

The type does most of the work. Cormorant Garamond, a light, high-contrast serif, for headings and the property names. Jost, a plain sans, very small and widely spaced, for labels. Sections are numbered in Roman numerals, I to VI, and photographs are called plates. It reads like a printed catalogue for a gallery more than an app, which is closer to how these homes are sold in person.

As on the earlier days, the page follows your phone or computer. If it is set to dark, the site opens dark. A round button in the header switches it, and the site remembers your choice next time.

The light theme: warm stone, ink and oxblood, with editorial serif type.

The dark theme. It follows the device until you choose, and the header button remembers.

the house

Section I is called The House, and it is one paragraph long. For more than a decade, Nina Estate has represented homes, buildings and investments across Málaga and the Costa del Sol, personally, and with discretion.

Three figures sit under it, each with a small label. 10+, years on the coast. One, point of contact. Four, disciplines. I wanted figures a client can check, not totals of square metres sold or a counter of happy families. The second one is the most important line on the page. At this level, a buyer wants to know that the person who answers the first call will still be there at the notary.

Follows your system setting, or pick one with the toggle.

four residences, not four hundred

Section II is the portfolio, under the plain heading Residences. Four filters sit on the right: all, Málaga, Marbella, investment. Choosing one rearranges the cards without reloading the page.

There are four properties in the concept. N°1, a villa in Marbella, 400 square metres. N°2, a building by the Cathedral in Málaga, sold whole. N°3, another building in the Centro Histórico. N°4, a residence in El Limonar, 329 square metres. Every one says price on request. The cards are large, set at different heights rather than in a tight grid, and each has one small arrow to open it.

Four is not many for a property website, and I left it at four. A long grid would make the business look like a portal, and it is not one. Under the cards is one line in italic: some of our finest homes are never published. Next to it is a button, request private access. In this part of the market, a lot of the best stock changes hands off-market, without a public listing. The page says so plainly and offers the way in.

Below that is a second full-width photograph, Plate II, with one line set over the quiet part of the image: discretion is not a service, it is the standard.

four disciplines, one at a time

Section III sets out the work in four parts: acquisition, sale, investment and rental. On the existing site, the services read as a list. Here each one is a row that opens in place, so a seller does not have to read past the buyer’s process to find their own.

Acquisition: a search shaped around how you wish to live, with every property vetted before it reaches you. Then brief and shortlist, accompanied viewings, negotiation, through to notary, and a button, begin a search. Sale: your property presented the way buyers at this level expect, and placed before the right people, with valuation, editorial photography, qualified buyers and discreet marketing. Investment: buildings, assets and income properties in the historic centre and along the coast, with whole buildings, yield analysis, off-portal opportunities and asset support. Rental: long-term lets handled for owners and tenants alike, with tenant selection, contracts and inventory, owner representation and relocation.

Each discipline ends with its own next step: begin a search, request a valuation, discuss an investment, enquire about rentals. Somebody who only came to sell never has to read about yields.

Each discipline opens in place, with its own services and next step.

the method

Section IV answers the question every first-time buyer in Spain asks sooner or later: what actually happens, and in what order? Four steps, numbered in small Roman numerals and set side by side.

Conversation: how you live, what you need, and the timeline you are working to. Selection: a short, considered list, with every property seen by the agency before you see it. Viewing: accompanied in person, or by private film around your schedule, which matters when the buyer lives in London or Dubai. Completion: negotiation, paperwork and notary, handled on your behalf through to the keys.

None of this is new to anyone who has bought property here. Written down in four short lines, it makes the process feel known before it starts, and for an expensive and slow decision that is a large part of what the client is paying for.

the person behind the business

Section V is the change I care most about. On a lot of agency websites the people are small photographs on an about page, if they appear at all. Here the director gets a section of her own, at the same size as the properties.

Jovana Dokic. Her name is set large, with the surname in italic, next to a portrait of her on a terrace above the port at dusk. The text is short: an expert in business and real estate, she leads Nina Estate with over a decade on the Costa del Sol, and every client works with her directly, in an integrated and personal service built to secure the best possible conditions. Under it are two buttons, message on WhatsApp and the phone number, +34 664 149 638.

The reason is practical. In a firm this size, the person is the service. Clients will speak to her, view with her and sign with her beside them. A website that hides that behind stock photos of keys and handshakes undersells the one thing a larger agency cannot easily copy.

The method in four steps, and the director, with a direct line to her.

by appointment

The last section, VI, is called private enquiries, and the heading reads by appointment. On the left are three ways in: the telephone, the email address, jovana@ninaestate.com, and the office on Avenida de Cánovas del Castillo 8, Málaga.

On the right is a short form. Name, email, telephone, a choice of what the enquiry is about, matching the four disciplines, and a message. Sending it opens the visitor’s email app with everything already written and addressed to Jovana. A line under the button says every enquiry is answered personally and in confidence. There is no client portal and no automatic reply that pretends to be a person. A private practice answers its own post.

on a phone

Many first contacts with an agency like this happen on a phone, at odd hours, from another country. A buyer in a hotel lobby looks up the agent a friend recommended. A seller abroad checks who they are about to call.

On a phone the residences stack one under another, each with its number, name, area, size and price on request, and a square arrow to open it. The filters wrap onto two lines rather than shrink. Both themes work the same way.

The menu opens over the whole screen. Five sections, numbered like the page: residences, services, the house, director, enquire. Below them are the two buttons someone on a phone actually uses, message on WhatsApp and the phone number, then the language choice and the theme switch. Everything a visitor needs to make contact fits on the first screen of the menu.

The residences on a phone, in both themes.

The full-screen menu: numbered sections, WhatsApp and phone, the language choice and the theme switch.

english and spanish

The people buying on this coast come from everywhere, and the people selling are often Spanish. The concept has EN and ES in the header and in the mobile menu from the start, because a practice like this needs both from the first day.

To be clear about what exists: the concept is written in English, and the Spanish switch is in place but the Spanish pages are not written yet. I would rather write them with the business than guess at how Jovana speaks to her Spanish clients.

an independent concept

Nina Estate did not hire me, and this is not their website. The properties, the director’s name and words, the phone, the email and the office are taken from what Nina Estate already publishes. I have not changed the facts. What I changed is the order, the tone and how the page looks: a private practice instead of a catalogue, the person at the front, and the process written down.

I have no figures on enquiries or sales, and I will not make any up. If nobody at Nina Estate wants it, the concept stays where it is as day four. If they do, the rest is practical: their own words in place of mine where I have filled in, the Spanish pages, every residence with its own page, the enquiry form sent wherever they want it, and the site moved onto ninaestate.com.

if your clients take months to decide

You may not sell property. Plenty of businesses sell something people decide on slowly: a school, a clinic, an architect, a lawyer, a yacht broker. The website is often built for quick decisions anyway, with grids, prices, counters and urgency.

For a slow decision it helps to do the opposite. Say who the client will deal with, and show them. Write the process down in a few steps. Show a small amount of work at a size where it can be looked at properly. Give one direct way to reach a person. Let the design be calm enough that the visitor reads instead of scrolls.

I am a web designer in Estepona, on the Costa del Sol, and I build websites like this one for businesses across Spain. If that sounds like your business, write to me from the main site. Tell me what you do and where, and I will reply in plain language. The concept is here, and Nina Estate’s own site is here, so you can compare the two. Four down, ninety-six to go.

entry.title: a seat at the long table
entry.summary: Day three of a hundred: a homepage concept for Los Arcos, a family bar and restaurant in Estepona, with the menu, the week, a booking request, and a light for lunch and one for late.
entry.content:
On 19 November I posted the third note of this run: a hundred days, a hundred businesses, a hundred websites, each one open to anyone. The first day was a family builder in the Marina Alta who needed a clear first page, something he could look at before a contract. That page is here. The second was a theatre in Málaga that already had a full season and needed an order a person could use. That one is here. Today the walk is shorter.

Los Arcos is a bar and restaurant on Calle Benavista, by exit 1057, in Estepona. I work from Estepona, so this is the first business in the run in my own town. That changes very little about the work and quite a lot about the care. People here will open the page and know whether it sounds like the place. You can open the concept here: Los Arcos, day three.

Nobody at Los Arcos asked me for it. It is not a commission and it is not their official site. Their name, their dishes and their week are on the page. The concept is mine, and for now it lives on my own address, the honest place for work nobody has adopted yet. I have not been told that anyone there has looked.

a place with more than one reason to come

The builder had one job to explain, and the theatre had a season. A family bar and restaurant has something less tidy. People come for different reasons, at different hours, often in the same group.

Someone wants a Sunday roast. Someone else wants the match on a big screen. A couple wants a cocktail and the band. A parent wants to sit down for an hour while the children run somewhere safe. On a weekday morning, someone just wants coffee and pancakes before work. Los Arcos does all of that under one roof: an open kitchen, the Sunday Carvery, a morning café, live sport, live music, play areas, takeaway.

A homepage that lists all of it at the same volume says nothing. One that picks a single reason leaves out half the people who already go. So the job was an order. First, what kind of place this is. Then what you can eat. Then what is on this week. Then when the doors are open, why it works for families, and how to get a table. Everything a regular already knows, in the order a newcomer needs it.

good food brings people together

The opening keeps their own line, because it is a good one: good food brings people together. It sits in a tall, narrow serif, with the second half in italic and in the house red. Above it is the logo, the arches with the little figures playing. Below, one paragraph: a family-style bar and restaurant, homemade food from an open kitchen, a traditional Sunday Carvery, fresh cocktails, a live band to sing along with, and plenty of room for the kids to play.

Then two buttons, book a table or see what’s on. Below them, three facts you might otherwise have to ask for: the Sunday Carvery at €15.95, the morning café from 8am Monday to Saturday, and the bar and restaurant from Wednesday to Sunday. A red band runs across the foot of the screen with the reasons people come, one after another: live music, fresh cocktails, play areas, takeaway, and the line about good food.

On the right, a large photograph of a platter: carved chicken, ribs, sausages, onion rings, a pot of beans, a dish of sauce. I wanted the first screen to look like a table, not a brochure.

The first screen, cut in two. The same opening by day and after dark.

two lights, one restaurant

That diagonal cut is the point of the concept. The page comes in two themes, and the same restaurant has to feel right in both.

The light one is warm cream, close to a tablecloth, with the brand red for anything you can press and for the italic words. It reads easily at noon on a terrace with the sun on the screen. The dark one is charcoal, almost black, with the same red. It is easier at ten at night, when someone is checking whether the kitchen is still open or sending the page to a friend from the sofa.

If your phone is already set to dark, the page opens dark. If it is set to light, it opens light. A small button in the navigation switches it, and the page remembers your choice next time. The cards, the photographs and the red stay the same. Only the room around them changes.

The light theme: warm cream, brand red, and the week in a grid.

The dark theme. It follows the device until you choose, and the toggle remembers.

from the open kitchen

A restaurant page is opened to see the food, so the food comes second, straight after the welcome. The heading says it plainly: from the open kitchen. One line underneath says the favourites are traditional, homemade and freshly prepared where you can see them.

Then a short list of six dishes, numbered like a menu card: T-Bone Steak, Butterfly Chicken Breast, Salmon Steak with Chilli Roast Potatoes, Chilli Con Carne, Sausage and Mash, Chocolate Fudge Cake. Each carries a small label: grill, fish, house, classic, dessert. Pick one and its photograph comes up beside the list. The T-Bone arrives on a wooden board with a round of herb butter melting on top.

Under the list, one sentence names the rest of the menu so nobody thinks those six are all there is: legendary ribs, beer-battered cod, sirloin, burgers, pizza, crisp and Caesar salads, a children’s menu, a specials board in the bar and food to take away. I have not eaten my way through it, so I will not describe the taste. The page describes the dishes as Los Arcos does, and puts the pictures where a hungry person will look.

what’s on, and when to find us

Next comes the week, because a bar like this lives by it. The heading is What’s on, and the grid is honest about booking: recommended for some things, essential for others.

The Sunday Carvery gets the red card: every Sunday, €15.95, a traditional Sunday lunch carved for the table. Beside it, the new morning café, half price on the café menu until Sunday 22 November for the launch, Monday to Saturday from 8am to 2pm and Sunday from 8am to noon. The Kids’ Christmas Party, Saturday 19 December from 2 to 5pm, has Santa’s grotto, entertainment and a buffet from 3 to 4pm, at €15 a child, booking essential. Christmas Day is four courses at €60, one long table, booking required. Then the screens, for the match with friends, family or colleagues and free WiFi at the tables. Then the bar, with a live band, fresh cocktails, and a note that weddings, birthdays and reunions are welcome.

Every card ends in one action: book Sunday, book places, reserve Christmas, plan a celebration. Nobody has to work out what to do next.

The hours follow, under When to find us. Three tabs, because Los Arcos keeps three kinds of hours: restaurant, bar and café. Choose one and the large line on the left tells you what matters right now, in Estepona time: open, or opens at 14:00, later today. On the right is the full week, with today marked in red. The restaurant is closed on Monday and Tuesday, open from 14:00 to 21:00 Wednesday to Friday, from 12:00 to 21:00 on Saturday and from 12:00 to 20:00 on Sunday. The small green dot in the navigation does the same job at a glance. It says café open when the café is open.

Pick a dish to see it. Pick restaurant, bar or café to see when it is open today.

room to play, time to relax

There is a section for families, because that is a large part of why people choose Los Arcos over the place next door. Room to play. Time to relax. Large play areas with equipment keep the children busy while the grown-ups settle in. Six short points sit in two columns: play areas, children’s menu, free WiFi, takeaway, daily specials, private events. Two photographs carry the rest, the climbing frame with its green slides and a row of cocktails, one bright blue. It is the same afternoon seen by two generations.

Under that, one sentence from a guest, Paula Parker: what a great place for families, or even just to sit and chill. I kept it to one quote, set large, with no stars and no counter. One real sentence does more than a carousel.

save us a seat

The booking section is called Save us a seat. On the left are the three ways to reach the restaurant, each one tappable: the phone, +34 618 254 622, the email, info@losarcosestepona.com, and the address, exit 1057, Calle Benavista. A short line says what anyone who runs a restaurant would tell you: for today, it is quickest to call.

On the right is the request form. First the occasion, as five buttons: lunch or dinner, Sunday Carvery, Christmas Day, Kids’ party, celebration. Then the date, a time that is only offered once a date is chosen, and the number of guests. Then name, phone, email and anything the kitchen should know. Press the button and your email app opens with the request already written, ready to send.

The concept does not pretend to be a booking system. There is no account, and the form says plainly that the booking is confirmed once the restaurant replies. On this coast, a table is still often agreed by phone or by a reply from the owner, and a page that promised more than that would be lying.

Choose the occasion, the date, the time and the guests. The request opens in your email, ready to send.

the same evening on a phone

Most people will meet this page on a phone. Someone parked outside wants to know whether the kitchen is open. A group chat is deciding where to watch the match. A parent is booking the children’s Christmas party in the five minutes between two other things.

On a phone everything stacks in the same order. The heading, the line, the photograph, and the dish name on a small label over the picture. The book button stays in the top bar, next to the theme toggle, where a thumb can reach it from anywhere on the page.

The menu opens over the whole screen. Seven links, numbered like the dishes: home, about, our menu, facilities, live sports, events, contact. At the bottom are the two things a person in a hurry wants, a book a table button and the phone number. It works the same in both lights.

The open kitchen on a phone, in both themes.

The full-screen menu: seven numbered links, a booking button and the phone, light or dark.

an offer, not a takeover

Los Arcos did not hire me. This is not their website, and nothing here means they have approved it. They already have a site, a phone that rings, regulars, and a Sunday that fills up. The dishes, the prices, the dates and the guest’s words on the page are theirs, not mine. What I added is an order, two lights, and a booking request that tells the truth about how a table gets confirmed.

I have no figures for covers or takings, and I will not invent any. If someone at Los Arcos opens the concept and wants nothing from me, that is a complete ending. If they want it, the rest is practical: their own photographs, their own words where mine are standing in, the hours kept up to date, the form sent to whoever answers bookings, and a domain in their name.

It follows your system setting, or you choose. One tap, and the choice is remembered.

if your place has many doors

You may not run a restaurant. A lot of businesses on this coast look more like Los Arcos than like a one-line company. A gym with a café. A beach club with a shop. A school with summer camps. People come in through different doors, at different hours, for different reasons, and the website usually tries to hold every door open at once.

What helps is an order, not more blocks. Say what the place is in one line. Show the thing people actually come for. Put the week where it can be read and the hours where they answer “now”. Make the way in, a phone, a form, a table, honest about what happens next. Then let the page follow the light the person is in.

I am a web designer in Estepona, on the Costa del Sol, and I build websites like this one for businesses across Spain. If that sounds like your business, write to me from the main site. Tell me what you do and where, and I will answer in plain language. The short public version of today is the note: day three of a hundred, a homepage for a family restaurant in my own town, light or dark, the guest choosing. The note is here. Tomorrow is another business, and another finished page.

entry.title: room for a whole season
entry.summary: Day two of a hundred: a homepage concept for Teatro Soho CaixaBank in Málaga, with the season, the tickets and a page you can read by day or after the show.
entry.content:
On 18 November I posted the second note of this run: a hundred days, a hundred businesses, a hundred websites, where anyone can open them. The previous day was a family builder in the Marina Alta who needed a first clear page, something finished he could look at before a contract. That page is here. Today the place is different, and the work changes with it.

Teatro Soho CaixaBank stands on calle Córdoba, in Málaga. I work from Estepona, on the same coast, close enough that I do not have to pretend Málaga is a trip. The theatre already has a season, a building people walk to, a name that carries, and several activities under one roof. It is not waiting for its first sentence online. What I made is a homepage for the life it already has, and you can open the concept here: Teatro Soho, day two.

Nobody at the theatre asked me for it. It is not a commission, and it is not affiliated with the theatre or with CaixaBank. Their name is on the page. The concept is mine, and for now it lives on my own address, which is the honest place for work nobody has adopted. I have not been told that anyone there has looked, and I will not write as if they had.

a house that is already full

The visitor from the previous day wanted to know whether a firm could be trusted with a house. Someone opening a theatre page usually wants a smaller answer, and wants it quickly: what is on this Saturday, whether there is dance, whether a seat is still free, and who is on the stage. The season is the thing on offer, and it changes while the person is still deciding.

The building holds more than a calendar. Beside the theatre sit Larios Pop del Soho, Soho Sounds Records, Teatro Soho televisión and the Fundación Teatral Antonio Banderas, plus sponsors, the week’s news, a phone number and a street a taxi can find. Crowd that onto one screen and nobody finishes it. Leave it out and the poster has nowhere to lead. The work is an order a person can use, and a first minute that feels like arriving. After that, the page has to say what is on, and how to get a ticket.

I did not invent the names, the dates or the partners. They are public, and they are what the concept shows. I have not sat through these performances, so this is an account of the page, not of the night.

the first minute

The opening is this season. Small type at the top reads Temporada 26/27 · Málaga. The name below is large, Teatro Soho, and the letters arrive one by one, the way a title comes up once a room has gone quiet. Behind it is the poster for El Gran Gatsby – El Show: gold lettering, two dancers, a line that Enrique Gasa Valga Dance Company presents the evening, and a round gold mark reading música en directo. Beside a thin rose line, a short paragraph says the house presents the 26/27 season: theatre, music, dance and circus, in the heart of Málaga.

Under that, a band of words keeps moving: Circo, Teatro, Música, Danza, and then the same four again. Move down the page and the band picks up a little. Stop, and it settles. I mean that as a curtain going up, a small change in the room. A slow light also shifts behind the poster, closer to light on a stage than to a row of slides.

The first screen. The season, the poster, and the name of the house.

The same opening exists in two lights, because people do not all read in the same place. One is soft mint, with rose kept for the small accents, easy in a bright café or on a sunny pavement. The other is a deep teal, closer to a darkened auditorium, pink used the way a house light is used. If the phone is already set dark, the page opens dark. One tap switches it, and the choice is remembered. The poster and the name stay put. Late at night the page does not glare, and at lunch you are not handed a black screen to fight.

One homepage, two lights. The season stays, and the room around it changes.

finding Saturday

Below the band the heading is plain on purpose: Espectáculos a la venta, shows on sale. Five chips sit under it: Todos, Teatro, Música, Danza, Circo. If you want dance on Saturday, you tap Danza and the rest steps back. That is the whole task, two taps, instead of a search through a list drawn for the box office rather than for the person holding the phone.

Each show is a poster, then the name, then the dates. El Gran Gatsby – El Show runs from 17 to 22 November, filed under dance and music, which agrees with the gold mark. La Cubana, La cuisine de ma cousine, runs from 25 November to 15 December, filed under theatre, on a bright pink card with a cook’s hat that belongs to that company and not to the Gatsby poster. The two can sit together. A house programming circus, flamenco, musicals and straight plays will look careless if every card is forced into one frame.

The grid holds a season around those two. Christmas at the Soho, with Antonio Banderas, is there from 25 to 28 December. Duck Pond, by Circa, falls on 19 and 20 December. January brings Mujer en cinta de correr sobre fondo negro, Hija de la Luna, and Flamenco en el Soho 2027 from 8 January to 19 March, including Rancapino Chico and, the next night, Farru with Duquende in Natural. I am listing what the page lists. There is no review here, and no sales figure, because I do not have either.

Shows on sale, on a phone. Choose dance, and the other cards step aside.

Open a card and the show comes forward with two routes, buy a ticket or read more. Further down, in type you cannot miss, the line says Compra de entradas. Halfway through, a visitor should not have to guess whether tickets are sold on this page. Buying points to the channels the house already uses. Reading more points to the theatre’s own page for that show. I am not opening a second box office.

On a phone the same visit happens in a short moment. Someone at dinner is checking Saturday, or someone a few streets from calle Córdoba is sending a poster to the person who has to agree. The menu tucks into one control: programme, news, contact, sponsors, discography. Filters stay large enough for a thumb, and posters stack as picture, name and dates. You do not pinch the screen, and you do not turn the phone sideways to read the name of the house. A phone also moves, from a bright street at noon to a dark seat after the curtain, which is why the two lights belong here.

the rest of the house

Calle Córdoba holds more than dates. A row called Destacados moves through three cards. Larios Pop del Soho, with Contrátanos and a photograph of an orchestra in coloured light. Soho Sounds Records, a mixing desk, enough to say a label lives in the building. The Fundación Teatral Antonio Banderas, on a card of its own. Each says saber más and links to the theatre’s pages. I kept the names apart, because one soft heading would have made the house look smaller than it is.

News follows, under Últimas noticias, with a way through to the rest. Three notes, dated, with photographs. On 17 November, the opening of El Gran Gatsby – El Show, dance, music and live voice. On 16 November, flamenco: Rancapino Chico, Farru, Águeda Saavedra, Juan Tomás de la Molía, Pedro el Granaíno and Daniel Casares. On 13 November, the Premio Andalucía Excelente, for the theatre’s cultural projection. I am repeating the page, not a night I attended. Dated news is how a homepage shows the week is happening, instead of leaving the place parked on a logo from a season already over.

Highlights and the latest news, in the mint theme. The ground stays quiet so the pictures can be read.

Then the page slows down on purpose. El teatro is one sentence, set large: a living theatre on calle Córdoba in Málaga, with Larios Pop del Soho, Soho Sounds Records, Teatro Soho televisión and the Fundación Teatral Antonio Banderas. The words come forward as you reach them. It is short because the season above has already introduced the house, and it is there both for someone who does not know the place and for someone who does.

The foot of the page is where the visit becomes practical. C/ Córdoba 13, 29001 Málaga, the phone 952 42 91 73, info@teatrodelsoho.com, and a link for how to arrive. Artistic projects write to direccion@teatrodelsoho.com. Legal notes, privacy, cookies, press access, and a channel for alerts, complaints and claims sit in a row you can scan. A small credit says the website is by me. I left it visible, so the page does not borrow the authority of a house that has not asked for the work.

The house in one sentence, tickets in large type, and an address a taxi can use.

partners, given a proper place

A venue like this lives with its partners. Sponsors have a grid of their own, logos on white cards with enough air to tell them apart, not a grey strip under the legal text. San Miguel, El Corte Inglés, Larios, Fundación Starlite, the foundation, Sierra Blanca and Iberia are among them. Under Amigos del teatro, the line names CEMAT, the club of business people in Málaga who are friends of the theatre, and the cards go on through local names: a hotel, El Pimpi, a hospital group, the technology park.

I do not know the agreements behind those marks, and I will not invent them. A dignified place, on this page, means large enough to read, still tappable when the logos fall into two columns on a phone, and not in charge of the season. The shows stay above. In the darker theme the same stretch sits on deep teal, with pink kept to the small labels. A phone already set to dark will open it that way. One tap brings the mint back, and the choice is remembered.

The dark theme. One tap switches it, and the choice is kept for the next visit.

an offer, not an announcement

The theatre did not hire me, and neither did CaixaBank. This is not an official page, and nothing on it means the house has approved the work. People already buy tickets by the routes the house uses. I worked from public names, public dates, and the way the theatre describes itself, a living house on calle Córdoba with those four activities beside it, so someone in Málaga could recognise the place.

There is no quote, because nobody there gave me one, and I have not been told they have seen it. There is no figure for seats or takings. If they open the concept and want nothing from me, that is a complete ending. The previous day’s page existed so a builder could say yes, or no, or change one part. This is the same kind of offer, made to a house that already has an audience.

if the place is already busy

You may not run a theatre. From Estepona, most months look more like this day than like the first. That builder needed a clear page which did not exist yet: the name, the work, the towns, a way to be reached that matches how people already get in touch. Many businesses are past that. People already come. The season, the menu or the list of jobs is real, and the website grew by addition, a new block whenever something started, a strip for every partner, and the reason for the visit sitting underneath.

A redesign can keep what people already like: the name on the door, the work itself, and the partners in a decent place instead of covering what you sell. The address and the phone stay where a person can act. What changes is the order. Saturday takes two taps, the ticket sits where the hand already is, and the light follows the phone, easy after a show and easy at noon. A new page can make a full business easier to move through, and leave the character where people already found it.

I am a web designer in Estepona, on the Costa del Sol, and I build websites like this one for businesses across Spain. If that is your situation, write to me from the main site. Say what you do, and where, and I will answer in plain language. The short public version of today is the note from the 18th: day two of a hundred, a homepage for this theatre, light or dark, the visitor choosing. The note is here. Tomorrow is another business, and another finished page.

entry.title: built before the yes
entry.summary: Day one of a hundred: a one-page website for Pedro Sánchez Construction, already live, so he can see his own finished site before any contract is signed.
entry.content:
On 17 November I posted a short note. Day one of a challenge I am doing in the open: a hundred days, a hundred businesses, a hundred websites. The first is a single page for Pedro Sánchez Construction, a family builder in the Marina Alta. It is already online.

I work from Estepona, on websites for shops, studios and trades. The site ought to behave like the business: clear about the work, and reachable on an ordinary afternoon. I built this one before anyone hired me.

You can open it here: Pedro Sánchez Construction, day one. It sits on my own address for now. That is the honest place until the owner takes it on.

a hundred days, one business at a time

One business a day, and a real website each time, not a picture saved for a meeting that might never come. After a hundred days I want a hundred pages a person can open and recognise. This builder is the first. Ninety-nine are still ahead.

The idea comes from Ramiah Trask. He thinks a run of days like this is a sound way to build a web design business, because of what it does for the client. Hiring usually means imagining a site that does not exist: other people’s pages, a proposal, your own name still on a blank. A finished page is smaller to decide about. You open it, see your towns and your work, and pass a phone across the table. Yes, or no, or change this part.

I have not spoken with Pedro. As far as I know he has not seen the page, and I will not pretend otherwise. It is there so he can look at something finished.

what a builder’s customers are looking for

The page presents a family firm that has been building homes in the Marina Alta for more than twenty-five years. It names Jávea, Dénia and Calpe, and the coast around them, on the Costa Blanca in Alicante. The line at the top is the one they lead with: more than twenty-five years building homes. New houses, full renovations, a close way of dealing with people, care with the detail.

I did not invent that history. Twenty-five years on the same coast is what a client listens for: the firm was here before this year’s kitchens, and may still answer if a job runs long. “Family” is spelled out as trato directo. You deal with them, not a switchboard.

The work sits in two kinds. New houses, some they develop themselves and some drawn for one client, finished so a person can live there. Full renovations, where they listen and then propose a way through. Electricity, plumbing and carpentry are included. That last line matters if you have ever renovated. There is a bad middle to those jobs, when the electrics are called somebody else’s problem and that somebody has not been booked. I am reporting what the page says. I have not stood on their sites.

The visitor I had in mind is in a particular week. A plot. A house that no longer fits. A kitchen they have disliked for years. They are comparing two or three firms, and they want plain answers. Can I trust these people with a house. Can I see the work. How do I reach them this week, without opening an account.

the first screen

The first words are large: “Más de 25 años construyendo hogares.” Behind them, a line drawing of a house, pale on a deep blue ground. Under the headline, new builds and full renovations in Jávea, Dénia, Calpe and the rest of the Marina Alta. A family company, direct dealing, each detail looked after.

Two buttons. Tell us about your project, or see the projects. Talk now, or look at houses first.

Four short facts run along the bottom. More than twenty-five years. A family firm, close and personal. The whole path from the project to the day the keys are handed over. The place itself: Marina Alta, Costa Blanca, Alicante. They sit where the eye lands before any scrolling.

On a phone the same screen stacks. Headline, a few lines, the button. The drawing stays, smaller, so it is still their page.

The opening of the page, on a large screen and on a phone.

the story, and the two kinds of work

Further down, a few paragraphs say who they are. More than twenty-five years building and developing homes in the Marina Alta. Their own developments, and new houses in different styles, finished so someone can live there. The people they employ handle the building and the paperwork of handing a home over. The heading calls them a respected name in house building. That claim is theirs. The page leaves it alone.

The mark is a PS monogram, the name, and the words construcción and Marina Alta. It says whose page this is, at the top, and again at the foot.

Then the services, under a heading that promises the whole job from start to end. Beside it, electricity, plumbing and carpentry included. Two photographs do the explaining. One is a single-storey house with a tiled roof, a pool, and a table under the trees: new construction, their own developments and houses made to measure. The other is a long covered room, arches along one side, a large woven lamp, the garden at the far end: renovations, where they listen and then propose. Small labels sit on the pictures for anyone in a hurry. New build, housing development, paperwork and handover. Full renovation, rehabilitation, kitchens and façades.

Under the photographs, the order a client lives. First they listen, because each project is its own. Then they propose. Then they carry the work out, from planning to the last day on site.

A short passage follows on living in the Marina Alta. Coves, mild winters, warm summers, food, and some quiet. Dénia, Jávea and Calpe are named on their own. Plenty of people commissioning a house here are choosing the town as well as the firm, so the page says so, briefly, and goes back to the work.

Who they are, and the two kinds of work: new houses, and full renovations.

the houses themselves

People trust a builder when they can see houses. The page shows three recent projects, each a photograph with a title and one line.

A white villa with a terrace, arches and a garden. A living room redone in natural tones: pale curtains, a low chair, wood, a lamp. A terrace and an outside stair still in the middle of the work, the coast behind them. That third one matters. A job in progress says renovation belongs here, not only the finished villas.

There is a way through to all the projects. On a phone the photograph comes before the label. I have not walked these rooms, so I will not invent how they feel. They are shown large, in ordinary Spanish. The word portfolio is not used. At a kitchen table, a client already says “projects”.

Recent work, as photographs with a title and one line each.

getting in touch

The end of the page is what makes the rest useful. You can write on WhatsApp, or fill in a short form: name, telephone, email, and what the project is. You tick that you have read the privacy note. The button says send by WhatsApp. WhatsApp then opens with your message already written, and you press send yourself. It does not disappear into an inbox nobody checks. You can see the next step.

Under the number, one line: write on WhatsApp or use the form, and they will reply. The heading above it is “leave your project in the hands of experts.” Along this coast a lot of arranging already happens on WhatsApp. A different number later is a small change.

the same page on a phone

A couple leaving a viewing. Someone sending a kitchen they want taken out to the person who has to agree. A name heard in Dénia, opened in a car park. The screen is narrow, and the moment is short.

The phone shows the same site. The opening line, both kinds of work with their photographs, electricity, plumbing and carpentry named above them, projects that still read as houses. The button sits where a thumb reaches it. The menu leaves once you have chosen. No pinching. No turning the phone sideways to make a sentence fit.

The same site on a phone: the opening, the services, and the projects.

what happens next with this site

It is ready to hand over. That was the reason for building it first. Someone at the company can open it today and say yes, or no, or yes if a few things move.

If they want it, the rest is practical. A domain in their own name, so the address is theirs. A sentence they would rather write themselves. A photograph they prefer. A project added, or taken down. Their words and their pictures, in the places where this page is standing in for a conversation we have not had. Then it goes live under their name, on their phone, answered their way.

Until that happens it stays where I put it. An open address, day one of the challenge, with no pretence that they have agreed. They have not told me they have looked. If you are Pedro, or you work there, I would rather hear “change that terrace” than hear nothing.

if you run a small business

You may not build houses. From Estepona I see the same bind most months. The business needs a website, or a better one than the page assembled in a hurry years ago. You are shown other trades and asked to picture your own. Often the price arrives first, and the decision is supposed to come out of a meeting.

It can go the other way. The page exists first: your name, the work you do, the towns you serve, a way to be reached that matches how you already talk to people. You open it on your phone. You show a partner, a sibling, the person who looks after the money. Then you decide.

That is the useful part of these hundred days, and it is how I prefer to work when no challenge is running. I am a web designer in Estepona, on the Costa del Sol, and I build websites like this one for businesses across Spain. If you want a page like that, write to me from the main site. Say what you do, and where. I will answer in ordinary language.

a small favour

This first site is for a company I would like to work with, and I have no side door in. If you know Pedro Sánchez, or someone at the firm, send them the page. That was the request in the note, and it still is: day one, written in public.

I will carry on. One business, one website, the next day. If the page finds its owner, good. If it only makes the second one clearer, that still counts.
